lessonTitle: Audit and Quality Improvement: Closing the Loop

blocks.text: On Ward 4, a pressure-ulcer risk assessment is meant to be completed within 6 hours of admission. A foundation doctor pulls 80 sets of notes and finds it was done for only 52. That single number is an audit. What happens next, whether the ward changes a process, tests it, measures again and tells others, is what turns a finding into quality improvement.

blocks.markdown: Clinicians constantly ask 'are we doing what we should?' and 'can we do it better?' Four activities are easily confused: **clinical audit**, **service evaluation**, **quality improvement (QI)** and **research**. They differ in purpose, in whether there is a standard to compare with, and in what approvals they need.

rows: Clinical audit
Are we meeting an agreed standard of care?
Explicit standard (guideline, policy), compared with practice
Local audit registration; ethical review not usually required
Service evaluation
What standard does this service achieve, or how is it experienced?
No external standard imposed; describes current practice
Local governance; usually no research ethics review
Quality improvement
How can we improve a process or outcome?
Aim and measures tracked over time through tested changes
Local governance; research ethics only if it meets the definition of research
Research
What is the best treatment or what is true in general?
Generates new generalisable knowledge; often allocates participants to different interventions
Research Ethics Committee review and Health Research Authority approval, sponsor, consent
blocks.caption: The Health Research Authority decision tool helps to classify a project. If in doubt, ask the clinical governance or research office before starting.

blocks.title: The audit cycle
blocks.text: A **clinical audit** measures practice against explicit criteria and standards, then changes practice where it falls short and re-measures to confirm improvement: (1) choose a topic and set the **criterion** and **standard** (for example 'risk assessment within 6 hours of admission; standard 95%'); (2) collect data; (3) compare with the standard; (4) implement change; (5) **re-audit** to close the loop. Audit data are collected from routine practice and patients are not allocated to different care for the project.

blocks.latex: \text{Compliance}=\frac{\text{number of cases meeting the criterion}}{\text{number of cases audited}}\times100\%
blocks.caption: The basic audit measure. The gap to the standard shows how many more patients must be compliant to reach it.

blocks.title: Reading an audit and closing the loop
blocks.prompt: Ward 4 audits 80 consecutive admissions against the standard that a pressure-ulcer risk assessment is completed within 6 hours; the standard is 95%. 52 admissions complied. After a change the ward re-audits another 80 admissions and 70 comply. Interpret the results.

steps.text: Gap to the standard: 95% of 80 is 76 admissions, so 24 more compliant admissions were needed.

Compliance improved by 22.5 percentage points but remains below the 95% standard (it still falls 6 admissions short of 76). The loop is therefore not fully closed: the ward should study why 10 admissions failed, adapt the change and re-audit, and should treat a single before-and-after comparison cautiously because it cannot prove that the change caused the improvement.

blocks.answer: 65% then 87.5% compliance (up 22.5 percentage points) but still below the 95% standard, so further cycles are needed.

blocks.markdown: **Is it research?** The key distinction is intention and design. Research aims to produce new, generalisable knowledge, usually with a protocol that may allocate participants to different interventions, and needs ethical review and consent. Audit and service evaluation look at local practice to improve it, using data already collected as part of care, though patient confidentiality and data protection still apply. If a project tests a new intervention in a way that goes beyond usual care, randomises patients or intends to publish generalisable findings, check with the research office; the label does not decide the matter, the features do.

blocks.title: Plan-do-study-act (PDSA)
blocks.text: **QI** uses the Model for Improvement: set a SMART aim (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), choose measures, and test changes in rapid, small **PDSA** cycles. **Plan**: decide the change, who, when, and *predict* the result. **Do**: carry it out on a small scale and record what happened, including problems. **Study**: compare the data with the prediction and reflect on what was learned. **Act**: adopt, adapt or abandon the change, then plan the next cycle. Use **outcome** measures (what we want to improve), **process** measures (whether the steps are done) and **balancing** measures (unintended consequences, such as time taken).

blocks.title: A PDSA cycle for Ward 4
blocks.prompt: The team's aim is to raise within-6-hour risk assessment compliance from 65% to 90% within 12 weeks. Describe cycle 1 and interpret its result.

steps.text: Plan: add a prompt to the admission checklist and ask the nurse in charge on the morning shift to use it for one week. Predict that compliance on that shift will reach at least 80%. Decide the measures: proportion of admissions assessed within 6 hours (process and outcome) and nurse time per admission (balancing).
Do: over the week 15 admissions occurred on the shift, and the team recorded each assessment time.

Study: compliance matched the prediction. The 3 misses were all admissions late in the shift, after 13:00, when the checklist was not available at the bedside. The balancing measure showed an average of 2 extra minutes per admission, judged acceptable.

Act: adapt rather than adopt. Cycle 2 will add the prompt to the afternoon, evening and night shifts with a named lead, retest for another week, and plot results on a run chart to see whether the change is real or normal variation.

blocks.answer: Cycle 1 achieved 80% as predicted, revealed a late-in-shift gap, and led to an adapted second cycle rather than ward-wide rollout.

blocks.markdown: **Run charts.** Plot the measure against time (for example weekly compliance) with the median of the baseline as a centre line. Because all processes vary, do not read two points as proof of change. A commonly used rule is that a **shift** of six or more consecutive points all above or all below the median suggests a real change, rather than random variation, as does a sustained run of rising or falling points. Annotate the chart with when each change was made.

**Presenting findings.** A poster or oral presentation must tell the audience what you did, what you found and what they should do. Lead with one clear message. For an oral summary of about five minutes, state the aim, give brief background, method (standard, sample, measures), results and the 'so what', with a single chart per key finding. Keep data honest: report the denominator, the standard used and limitations, do not show identifiable patient information, and acknowledge the team and any funding.

rows: Title and authors
Topic and key message; team and affiliation
Make the title a statement of the result where possible
Aim and background
Why the topic matters; the standard or evidence
Two or three lines; cite the standard
Methods
Standard, sample, data source, change tested, measures
Brief and reproducible; state the audit criteria or PDSA cycle design
Results
Run chart or bar chart with numerators and denominators
One clear graph; label axes; show the target
Conclusions and recommendations
What it shows, limits, next steps
Link back to the aim; say who will act and when
Acknowledgements
Team, patients, funders; ethics or governance statement
Be transparent about governance status
blocks.caption: A typical audit or QI poster layout. Text should be brief and legible from a distance.

blocks.title: Common pitfalls
blocks.text: Calling research an audit to avoid ethical review is a breach of governance. Measuring without a standard, changing many things at once, or not re-measuring leaves the loop open. Percentages without denominators, charts with truncated axes and conclusions that overreach the data mislead the audience.

points: Audit compares practice with an explicit standard and re-audits after change; service evaluation describes a service without an external standard; research generates new generalisable knowledge and needs ethical review.
QI uses an aim, outcome, process and balancing measures, and PDSA cycles that test changes on a small scale and predict the result.
Run charts help distinguish real change from random variation; compliance is numerator over denominator and compared with the standard.
Presentations should state the message, aim, methods, results with denominators, conclusions and limitations, with honest, anonymised data.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor checks whether 50 consecutive patients on a ward had a falls risk assessment within 24 hours of admission, as required by the hospital policy. How should this project be classified?

options.text: Qualitative study, because the notes are text
Randomised trial, because 50 patients were included
Clinical audit, because practice is compared with an explicit standard
Research requiring ethics committee review, because patient data were used

questions.correctOptionText: Clinical audit, because practice is compared with an explicit standard

distractorRationale.a: The activity measures compliance with a standard, which is not qualitative research.
distractorRationale.b: Patients were not allocated to different interventions.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: measuring practice against a defined standard is audit.
distractorRationale.d: Using routine data to compare with a standard for local improvement is generally audit, not research.

questions.explanation: An audit asks whether care meets an agreed standard and uses routinely collected data without changing what patients receive. Here the policy is the standard and the project measures compliance, so it is a clinical audit.

questions.stem: A team plans to randomise 200 patients with chronic wounds to one of two dressings to decide which heals faster, intending to publish the results so other hospitals can use them. How should this be classified and managed?

options.text: As clinical audit, because it takes place in a hospital
As service evaluation, which needs no approval
As QI, since any change in wound care is QI
As research, requiring a protocol, ethics committee review, sponsor and informed consent

questions.correctOptionText: As research, requiring a protocol, ethics committee review, sponsor and informed consent

distractorRationale.a: The setting does not determine the category.
distractorRationale.b: Allocating patients to different interventions to generate new knowledge goes beyond service evaluation.
distractorRationale.c: QI tests changes locally and does not typically randomise patients to produce generalisable knowledge.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: randomisation, generalisable aims and publication make it research.

questions.explanation: Features of research include random allocation to interventions and the aim of producing generalisable knowledge. It needs Research Ethics Committee and HRA approval, a sponsor and participant consent, and should not be labelled audit to avoid them.

questions.stem: A clinic manager asks you to describe how long patients currently wait at each step of the clinic and how satisfied they are, with no target standard and no change planned. What is this best called?

options.text: Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
Systematic review
Clinical audit

distractorRationale.a: There is no allocation to interventions.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it describes how a current service operates without an external standard.
distractorRationale.c: There is no synthesis of published studies.
distractorRationale.d: There is no explicit standard being measured against.

questions.explanation: Service evaluation measures how a service is delivering or being experienced without comparing it to a specified standard or testing a new intervention. Audit requires a standard; research requires generalisable aims.

questions.stem: A ward tests a new handover checklist with one nurse during one shift, records how it went and compares it with the team's prediction before deciding what to do next. At which PDSA stage is the comparison with the prediction made?

options.text: Act
Do
Study
Plan

distractorRationale.a: Act decides to adopt, adapt or abandon after the study.
distractorRationale.b: Do is carrying out the test and recording observations.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the Study stage analyses results against the prediction and reflects on what was learned.
distractorRationale.d: Planning sets the change and the prediction, before the test.

questions.explanation: In PDSA, Plan defines the change and predicts the result, Do runs the test on a small scale, Study compares the results with the prediction and reviews learning, and Act decides to adopt, adapt or abandon. Small, quickly repeated cycles reduce risk and allow learning.

questions.stem: In a plan-do-study-act approach, a new change is usually first tested on a small scale before being rolled out more widely.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Small-scale tests limit risk, give rapid feedback and allow the change to be adapted before wider implementation. Several cycles with increasing scale build confidence that the change works in different conditions.

questions.stem: A trainee presents an audit as a poster. Which design best communicates the findings?

options.text: Percentages without the sample size, to keep it simple
A clear message in the title, the standard stated, results shown as a labelled chart with numerators and denominators, and conclusions tied to the aim
Dense paragraphs of text, with no figures, so that detail is complete
Patient names and photographs to make the cases vivid

questions.correctOptionText: A clear message in the title, the standard stated, results shown as a labelled chart with numerators and denominators, and conclusions tied to the aim

distractorRationale.a: Omitting denominators prevents the reader from judging reliability.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it presents a focused, transparent, honest summary.
distractorRationale.c: Dense text is hard to read and the key findings are lost.
distractorRationale.d: Identifiable information breaches confidentiality and data protection.

questions.explanation: A good poster or oral summary has one clear message, brief methods, a legible chart with denominators, and conclusions that follow from the data and state limitations. Patient information must be anonymised.

questions.stem: An audit standard states that 90% of patients on anticoagulants should have a documented bleeding-risk assessment. An audit of 140 sets of notes finds that 98 are compliant. How many additional compliant patients (out of the 140) would have been needed to meet the standard?
questions.explanation: The standard requires $0.90\times140=126$ compliant patients. Compliance was $98/140=70\%$, so $126-98=28$ more compliant patients were needed. Presenting the gap in patients as well as percentage points helps a team see the size of the task.

questions.stem: A team plots weekly compliance (%) on a run chart. The baseline values over 7 weeks are 58, 64, 61, 66, 59, 63, 62. Calculate the median, which will be used as the centre line, in percent.
questions.explanation: Sorted, the values are 58, 59, 61, 62, 63, 64, 66; the middle (fourth) value is 62%. After the change, six or more consecutive weekly points above this median would suggest a real shift rather than random variation, whereas one or two high points would not.

questions.stem: Distinguish clinical audit, service evaluation, quality improvement and research. For each, state the central question and whether research ethics review is normally required, using one example.
markingGuide: Audit: measures practice against an explicit standard and re-audits; for example compliance with a policy; ethics review not normally required
Service evaluation: describes how a service is performing or experienced without an external standard; usually no research ethics review
QI: tests changes using an aim, measures and PDSA cycles to improve local processes; governance but not usually research ethics
Research: aims to produce new generalisable knowledge, often with allocation to interventions; requires REC and HRA approval, sponsor and consent
Intention, design and generalisability decide the category; use HRA decision tool and ask governance
Confidentiality and data protection apply to all
questions.explanation: The categories differ in purpose and in whether a standard or new knowledge is the goal. Research that tests interventions or aims for generalisable findings needs formal ethical approval, whereas audit, service evaluation and QI are local improvement activities with governance oversight but not usually ethical review.

questions.stem: Discharge summaries on a medical ward are often sent to GPs more than 48 hours after discharge. Design a QI project to improve this: write an aim, choose outcome, process and balancing measures, describe the first PDSA cycle, and explain how you would present the results in a five-minute oral summary.
markingGuide: SMART aim with baseline, target and time frame (for example proportion sent within 24 hours)
Outcome measure: proportion of summaries sent within the target; process measure: completion of summaries at time of discharge; balancing measure: clinician time or errors in the summary
PDSA cycle 1: small test (one team or day), with a prediction, data collection, review and adapt
Plot weekly data on a run chart with a baseline median and annotate changes
Oral presentation: aim, background, method, results chart with denominators, conclusions, limitations and next steps
Honest, anonymised data; acknowledge the team
questions.explanation: A QI project needs a measurable aim and a set of balanced measures, and it tests changes in small PDSA cycles with predictions. Results are tracked on a run chart and presented simply, with denominators and limitations, so the audience can see what was learned and what should happen next.
